extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and policymakers (late 18th-century readers sympathetic to conservative critique of the French Revolution)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century political reflection arguing against the confiscation of Church and private property and warning of the political and moral consequences of revolutionary finance and institution-breaking. Aimed at persuading the British public and legislators to resist similar measures at home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for property rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The seizure or confiscation of private and ecclesiastical property is an outrage on all the rights of property and tantamount to tyranny; property established under law, usage, and long prescription should be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that taking property 'unaccused, unheard, untried, by whole descriptions, by hundreds and thousands together' is tyrannical; confiscation cannot be justified by novel political doctrines ('the rights of men') and is condemned even when cloaked in pretexts like 'national faith.' Examples: the seizure of Church revenues in France, turning tenants and clergy into dependents on atheistic charity. Anti-patterns: using abstract political formulas to override long-established legal titles and accumulated possessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process and noncollective punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Men should not be deprived of property or cast down to indigence and contempt without accusation, hearing, or trial; collective punishment of classes is unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke emphasizes that seizing property en masse of a class (e.g., clergy or nobility) without individual culpability is worse than robbery; degradation and social infamy imposed without legal process is a cruelty often worse than death. Use of formal legal-sounding acts to effect mass dispossession is a sham when substantive due process is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: The legal personality and rights of ecclesiastics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastics are real persons with legitimate legal and proprietary interests, not mere 'fictitious persons' created by the state to be dissolved at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke rejects the argument that clergy are constructs of the state whose goods belong to the state; he points to law, usage, court decisions, and long prescription as foundations of their rights. Anti-patterns: declaring occupational or corporate personhood null to justify arbitrary appropriation of assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of private claims over public creditors
rubrics_metrics.description: The first civil faith is pledged to the property of citizens, not to public creditors; creditors of the state have claim only on the public estate, not on private fortunes unless so contracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke draws on Necker's budget to argue that it was never intended that the state's creditors could seize private estates as security; the public can pledge only what is public revenue raised by just and proportioned imposition upon citizens. Anti-patterns: treating individual private property as valid collateral for public debt by revolutionary fiat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional and equitable taxation as remedy for public debt
rubrics_metrics.description: If deficits exist, the proper remedy is moderate, proportioned assessment on citizens generally, not targeted confiscation of particular classes' property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Necker's figures, Burke argues a modest, equitable contribution could have covered the deficit; the clergy and nobility had already contributed by various indirect taxes and other means. Guidance: prefer broad-based, proportionate impositions rather than partial confiscations that are oppressive and politically motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicion of ulterior motives when policy disproportionately benefits a faction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a measure (e.g., confiscation) disproportionately benefits a particular new interest (moneyed, municipal, or stockholder classes), it should be suspected as motivated by factional self-interest rather than necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contends that confiscation of Church lands served to create and enrich a 'new moneyed interest' and bind municipalities and financiers to the new regime. Example: refusal to accept an extravagant ransom from the clergy because it would have prevented creation of the new landed interest. Anti-patterns: policymaking that cloaks rent-seeking as public necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in disposal of large landed estates
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden, wholesale flood of church and crown lands on the market would depress land values and damage the economy; sale must be managed with regard to broader market effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke explains that immediate mass sale would devalue all landed property and divert circulating capital from trade to land; alternatives considered included exchange for stock or staged sales, but those posed equal or other difficulties. Guidance: account for market liquidity and systemic impacts when disposing of major asset classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to creating paper currency and forced circulation as a cover for plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing new paper currency founded on eventual sale of confiscated property, and making such paper compulsory in payments, is a means to force participation in and support of a spoliation scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke describes the creation of a new 3% debt and paper currency to satisfy demands of the 'bank of discount' and to bind municipalities to the spoil; making the currency compulsory coerced reluctant parties into complicity. Anti-patterns: compulsory acceptance of fiat instruments tied to expropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The danger of literary and opinion monopolies in political change
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of avenues to opinion (writers, academies, encyclopædia) allied with moneyed interests can prepare and justify radical measures against institutions like the Church and aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that a 'literary cabal' and men of letters, united with financiers, spread proselytising zeal, discredit opponents, and normalize radical actions. Guidance: scrutinize the formation of intellectual monopolies and their role in legitimizing policy shifts; anti-patterns include the use of satire and polemic to erase plural reputation and justify persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and reciprocity in public faith and treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: A new government ought to consider which acts and treaties of a prior government it will honor; arbitrary acceptance of some obligations (e.g., pecuniary) while rejecting others is inconsistent and suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes the Assembly only holds royal pecuniary engagements valid but rejects other royal acts; such selective acceptance reveals partiality and undermines honorable public faith. Guidance: evaluate legitimacy of a regime's chosen continuities and breaks in obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of independent judicature to check governmental power
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolition of independent courts (Parliaments) eliminates a check on central power and facilitates arbitrary rule and confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues the old Parliaments, despite faults, offered a locus for redress and rallying to ancient laws; their abolition enabled dictators in Paris to smooth the path for spoliation. Guidance: preserve judicial independence to protect property and civil rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral critique of political sophistry and rhetorical pretexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling tyrannical acts by high-sounding terms (philosophy, light, liberality, the rights of man) is rhetorical sophistry that masks theft and iniquity; evaluate policies by their effects, not their slogans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke repeatedly exposes how grand phrases were used as incantations to effect robbery (e.g., tying 'rights of men' to confiscation). Guidance: beware of moral/ ideological language used to justify substantive injustice; look for underlying means and ends.
